courses.title: Multilateral Diplomacy and Conference Craft
courses.description: How multilateral conferences actually produce texts: agendas, drafting groups, coalitions, chairing and the management of crisis diplomacy inside institutional settings.
objectives: Explain how multilateral conferences are structured
Draft operative paragraphs that survive negotiation
Manage coalitions and group politics
Chair a working group to a written outcome

modules.t: From Vienna to the United Nations
modules.i: Multilateral method emerged as a way of managing systemic war and technical cooperation.
o: Trace the development of conference diplomacy
modules.a: Compare decision rules at Vienna 1815 and San Francisco 1945 and explain the shift.
modules.l: Multilateralism changed the unit of legitimacy from dynastic agreement to collective membership. Majority voting made decisions possible at scale but created the permanent tension between legitimacy and great-power consent.

modules.i: Agenda, credentials, rules of procedure and time decide more than rhetoric.
r: Course pack: rules of procedure extract
modules.a: Draft an agenda and speaking order for a two-day conference on a supplied topic.
modules.l: Procedural questions are substantive: whoever controls the agenda controls what can be decided. Experienced delegations spend their preparation on procedure because it constrains every later move.

modules.i: Text is the currency of multilateral diplomacy.
o: Identify ambiguity as a negotiating device
modules.a: Draft three operative paragraphs on a contested issue and mark the likely objections.
modules.l: Preambular text establishes authority; operative text allocates obligation. Ambiguity is often deliberate, letting parties sign a text they read differently until implementation forces the question.

modules.i: Blocs negotiate internally before they negotiate externally.
r: Course note on UN voting groups
modules.a: Map the likely coalitions on a supplied issue and identify the pivotal broker.
modules.l: Formal groups reduce transaction costs but constrain members' flexibility. The pivotal actor is rarely the largest coalition; it is the one whose support makes a majority without requiring others to move.

modules.i: The chair's choices shape both process and substance.
modules.a: Write a chair's note summarising positions and proposing a way forward.
modules.l: A chair who summarises positions credibly becomes the reference point for the negotiation. The single text is the strongest tool available, but it costs the chair neutrality, which is why it is used late.

modules.i: Leaders' meetings compress negotiation and raise the cost of failure.
r: Case study: a bilateral summit package
modules.a: Prepare a summit deliverables list with owners and deadlines.
modules.l: Summits succeed on preparation: leaders sign what officials have already settled. Their value lies in the political cover they provide for difficult domestic decisions, not in the conversations themselves.

modules.i: Managing escalation under uncertainty is the hardest diplomatic skill.
r: Case study: a crisis management timeline
modules.a: Design a communication channel and message sequence for a supplied crisis.
modules.l: In crisis, ambiguity is costly: signals are read as intentions even when they are accidents. Dependable channels reduce the chance that a misunderstanding becomes a decision.

modules.i: Students negotiate a draft resolution under a mandate and a clock.
o: Negotiate a text from positions to adoption
r: Simulation pack: mandates and draft text
modules.a: Negotiate and submit the final text with a delegation report.
modules.l: The exercise tests whether a delegation can trade substance without losing its red lines. Success is measured by the text adopted and by the clarity of the reasoning in the report, not by rhetorical performance.

courses.title: Academic English for International Studies
courses.description: Academic reading, writing and speaking for students of international affairs, from argument structure and citation to seminar presentation in an academic register.
objectives: Read and summarise academic texts accurately
Build a coherent written argument with evidence
Cite sources correctly and avoid plagiarism
Deliver a clear academic presentation

modules.i: Academic texts have predictable architecture that can be read strategically.
o: Identify thesis and evidence in a text
modules.a: Annotate one article for thesis, evidence and counter-argument.
modules.l: Academic reading is a search for the argument, not a march through sentences. Locating the thesis and its evidence first makes the details interpretable, and shortens reading time considerably.

modules.i: An argument is a chain of claims each supported by evidence.
r: Course reader: model essay with margin notes
modules.a: Rewrite a supplied paragraph so that each sentence supports one claim.
modules.l: Weak academic writing usually lacks a claim rather than vocabulary. A paragraph should assert one thing, evidence it, and connect it to the next, so that the reader can reconstruct the reasoning without effort.

modules.i: Compressing a source without distorting it is a core academic skill.
modules.a: Summarise a two-page source in 120 words and paraphrase three sentences.
modules.l: Patchwriting, stitching source phrases into new sentences, is the most common inadvertent plagiarism. Genuine paraphrase reconstructs the meaning in your own syntax and always cites the source.

modules.i: Citation is a system for making claims verifiable.
modules.a: Format a reference list for five supplied sources in the required style.
modules.l: Consistency matters more than style choice: a reader must be able to trace every claim. Self-plagiarism and undisclosed assistance breach integrity just as clearly as unattributed copying.

modules.i: Academic English marks certainty carefully.
r: Swales, Academic Writing for Graduate Students, ch. 4
modules.a: Rewrite five overgeneralised sentences with appropriate hedging.
modules.l: Hedging is not weakness but calibration: it states how far the evidence supports the claim. Systematic overclaiming is one of the fastest ways to lose credibility in academic writing.

modules.i: Note-taking is an active process of structuring information.
r: Course reader: lecture recording with transcript
modules.a: Take notes on the supplied lecture and submit a one-page reconstruction.
modules.l: Effective notes record structure rather than transcription: headings, claims and examples. Signposting phrases signal those transitions, so listening for them converts a stream of speech into an outline.

modules.i: Describing charts precisely prevents misleading an audience.
modules.a: Write a 150-word commentary on a supplied chart.
modules.l: Data commentary moves from pattern to interpretation to caveat. Stating the source and the limits of the series is not optional: it is what makes the interpretation responsible.

modules.i: The module ends with a short assessed presentation and peer feedback.
modules.a: Deliver a ten-minute presentation on your essay topic and give peer feedback.
modules.l: A presentation is an argument delivered aloud, so structure matters more than completeness. Slides carry evidence, not the script, and the question period is graded as part of the presentation.

courses.title: Russian for Professional Diplomacy
courses.description: Applied Russian for diplomatic work: formal register, correspondence, meeting note-taking, treaty vocabulary and interpreting practice at intermediate level.
objectives: Use formal diplomatic register accurately
Draft routine diplomatic correspondence in Russian
Interpret between Russian and English in structured settings
Handle numbers, dates and treaty terminology

modules.i: Russian diplomatic language has fixed conventions of address and courtesy.
modules.a: Rewrite three informal messages in formal diplomatic register.
modules.l: Register errors carry more weight than grammar errors in diplomatic correspondence. Fixed formulae exist precisely to remove ambiguity about respect and hierarchy, so they should be reproduced, not improvised.

modules.i: Notes and letters follow structural conventions that must be reproduced exactly.
o: Use standard opening and closing formulae
r: Course pack: specimen notes with glosses
modules.a: Draft a note verbale requesting consular assistance.
modules.l: Correspondence templates encode relationships: third-person notes signal routine business, while first-person letters signal personal engagement. Choosing the template is choosing the relationship.

modules.i: Interpreting notes must capture argument, not transcript.
modules.a: Take notes on a five-minute speech and reconstruct it in Russian.
modules.l: Consecutive notes record the logic of a speech through symbols and links. Numbers, names and negations are the elements that must be written verbatim, because no context will recover them if lost.

modules.i: Precision with figures and legal terms prevents consequential errors.
o: Read large numbers and dates aloud
modules.a: Complete the numbers and dates drill and the terminology matching exercise.
modules.l: Number declension and date formulation are the commonest source of embarrassing error. Treaty vocabulary must be memorised in pairs, because near-synonyms in legal Russian have distinct legal effects.

modules.i: Running a meeting requires procedural language under time pressure.
o: Use procedural phrases to open and manage a meeting
modules.a: Chair a five-minute mock meeting using the phrasebook.
modules.l: Procedural formulae are the scaffolding of a meeting: they allocate the floor and record decisions. A chair who controls them can keep a discussion on time without appearing to silence anyone.

modules.i: Media Russian differs from official Russian in vocabulary and stance.
modules.a: Summarise two reports on the same event and note the framing differences.
modules.l: Media language encodes evaluation through word choice and attribution. Comparing two reports of one event trains the reader to notice framing that a single text conceals.

modules.i: Consecutive interpreting under realistic conditions.
modules.a: Complete the recorded consecutive interpreting exercise and self-assess.
modules.l: Interpreting is reformulation, not word substitution: the interpreter must deliver the speaker's meaning in the target register. Accuracy of content and consistency of register are assessed separately.

modules.i: Students brief and answer questions in Russian.
r: Simulation pack: brief and role cards
modules.a: Deliver a press statement and take three questions.
modules.l: A briefing succeeds when the same three messages survive every question. Deflection is a legitimate technique as long as it is courteous and does not appear evasive.

courses.title: International Security Studies
courses.description: Core concepts of security from deterrence and alliances to terrorism, cyber and energy security, with a sustained focus on how threats are constructed and securitised.
objectives: Apply deterrence theory to contemporary cases
Assess alliance and arms control dynamics
Analyse non-traditional security threats
Evaluate securitisation as an analytical framework

modules.i: What counts as a security issue is itself a political question.
o: Distinguish traditional from critical security studies
r: Buzan, Waever and de Wilde, Security: A New Framework for Analysis, ch. 2
Wolfers, 'National Security as an Ambiguous Symbol'
modules.a: Take one issue and argue whether it should be treated as a security matter.
modules.l: Securitisation theory treats security as a speech act: an issue becomes a security problem when an audience accepts the claim that it justifies exceptional measures. That move legitimates action but also narrows deliberation.

modules.i: Deterrence rests on credibility rather than capability alone.
modules.a: Assess whether a described threat posture is credible and explain the weakest link.
modules.l: Deterrence fails either because the threat is not believed or because the commitment is doubted. Extended deterrence is hardest, since it requires convincing an adversary that an ally's fate justifies existential risk.

modules.i: Arms control manages competition rather than ending it.
r: Course note on Cold War arms control
modules.a: Design an arms control measure for a supplied scenario and specify verification.
modules.l: Arms control aims at stability, not virtue: it constrains the weapons that create first-strike incentives. Verification is the load-bearing element, because an unverified limit is only an intention.

modules.i: Alliances aggregate power and generate commitment problems.
r: Walt, The Origins of Alliances, ch. 2
modules.a: Evaluate a burden-sharing dispute using capability and commitment data.
modules.l: Alliances persist after their founding threat fades because institutions build their own constituencies. Expansion extends protection but lengthens the frontier of commitment, raising the credibility problem.

modules.i: Asymmetric actors exploit the vulnerabilities of superior conventional forces.
modules.a: Assess two counter-terrorism measures against effectiveness and rights costs.
modules.l: Definitional disputes over terrorism are political because the label determines legal consequences. Counter-terrorism trades security gains against rights and legitimacy, and the trade-off must be argued explicitly.

modules.i: Cyber operations blur attack, espionage and preparation.
r: Case study: a critical infrastructure incident
modules.a: Analyse a cyber incident for attribution difficulty and escalation risk.
modules.l: Cyber deterrence is complicated by attribution: a threat is only credible if the actor can be identified and punished. Persistent engagement lowers the threshold for action, which raises escalation risk in turn.

modules.i: Security and energy intersect through dependence and infrastructure.
r: Course note on gas transit disputes
modules.a: Rank three diversification options for a dependent importer and justify the order.
modules.l: Energy security spans price, volume and political risk. Diversification improves resilience but is slow and capital-intensive, so states often accept political dependence while announcing long-run alternatives.

modules.i: Coercion below the threshold of armed attack tests existing frameworks.
modules.a: Propose a response to a supplied grey-zone campaign and defend the choice of instrument.
modules.l: Grey-zone activity exploits the gap between the prohibition on force and the reality of coercion. Because responses must remain below thresholds, resilience measures often outperform military signalling.

courses.title: Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
courses.description: The nuclear non-proliferation regime and its instruments: the NPT, IAEA safeguards, test bans, chemical and biological conventions, verification, and the practice of treaty negotiation.
objectives: Explain the NPT's bargain and its tensions
Apply IAEA safeguards concepts
Evaluate verification and compliance mechanisms
Negotiate a treaty text in simulation

modules.i: The technology that made strategy existential.
modules.a: Explain why survivable second-strike forces change crisis behaviour.
modules.l: Nuclear weapons altered strategy by making decisive victory self-defeating. Once second-strike forces are survivable, coercion shifts from defence to the manipulation of risk, which is the foundation of modern deterrence.

modules.i: A treaty built on a bargain between disarmament, non-proliferation and peaceful use.
r: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, Articles I-VI
Course note on review conference outcomes
modules.a: Analyse one compliance dispute under the NPT's institutional machinery.
modules.l: The NPT rests on a bargain whose three parts are unequally implemented, which is why review conferences are contentious. The withdrawal clause is its structural weakness: exit is legal, though politically costly.

modules.i: Verification converts a political commitment into technical procedure.
r: Course note on the Additional Protocol
modules.a: Design a safeguards approach for a hypothetical fuel-cycle facility.
modules.l: Safeguards verify declared material and, under the Additional Protocol, probe for undeclared activity. The gap between detection and enforcement is the regime's central political problem.

modules.i: Treaty design responds to verification capability.
r: Course note on bilateral arms treaties
modules.a: Evaluate whether a test ban can be verified, citing the monitoring system.
modules.l: Entry-into-force conditions that require hold-out states make ambitious treaties fragile. Verification technology is often ahead of political willingness, which leaves treaties in force-but-incomplete states.

modules.i: Two prohibitions with very different verification histories.
modules.a: Compare the verification strength of the two regimes and explain the difference.
modules.l: The CWC has intrusive verification because chemical production is detectable; the BWC lacks it because biological research is ubiquitous and dual-use. The difference is technical, but its consequence is political.

modules.i: Delivery systems complicate the proliferation picture.
o: Analyse the relationship between missiles and weapons
r: Course note on export control enforcement
modules.a: Assess a hypothetical export licence application against control list criteria.
modules.l: Export controls target the enabling technology rather than the weapon, which makes them broad but leaky. Effectiveness depends on enforcement and on the supplier's willingness to forgo revenue.

modules.i: Institutions must distinguish cheating from ambiguity.
modules.a: Design an inspection protocol for a supplied scenario and state its blind spots.
modules.l: Verification produces evidence; compliance is a political judgement about that evidence. Institutions therefore need both technical capability and a decision rule for acting on ambiguity.

modules.i: Students negotiate a short instrument under verification constraints.
r: Simulation pack: draft articles and mandates
modules.a: Negotiate and submit an agreed instrument with an explanatory report.
modules.l: Treaty negotiation is a package deal: verification depth is traded against participation breadth. The report must explain why each compromise was necessary, since the text alone cannot show it.

courses.title: Research Design in the Social Sciences
courses.description: How to turn an interest into a researchable question and a defensible design, covering concepts, measurement, case selection, qualitative and basic quantitative methods, and research ethics.
objectives: Formulate a researchable question
Operationalise concepts into measurable indicators
Justify a case-selection strategy
Write an ethics-aware research proposal

modules.i: A good question is answerable, consequential and bounded.
r: King, Keohane and Verba, Designing Social Inquiry, ch. 1
modules.a: Turn three broad topics into researchable questions and rank them by feasibility.
modules.l: A question earns its place by connecting to a puzzle in the literature and by being answerable with available evidence. Questions that cannot fail are not research questions but positions.

modules.i: Concepts must be defined before they can be measured.
r: Adcock and Collier, 'Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard'
modules.a: Operationalise one concept with two indicators and compare their validity.
modules.l: Measurement error enters at the point of conceptualisation: if the concept is vague, no indicator can rescue it. Validity asks whether the indicator captures the concept; reliability asks whether it does so consistently.

modules.i: Cases are chosen to make inferences, not for convenience.
o: Explain selection on the dependent variable
r: Course note on selection on the dependent variable
modules.a: Choose two cases for a supplied question and defend the comparison.
modules.l: Case selection is an inference strategy: comparison identifies the effect only if the cases vary on the right dimensions. Selecting cases by outcome destroys the variation the design needs.

modules.i: Interviews, documents and observation each produce different evidence.
r: Course note on coding and intercoder reliability
modules.a: Draft an interview guide for your proposal and pilot it on a peer.
modules.l: Qualitative evidence is strongest when triangulated: an interview claim confirmed by a document and an observation carries more weight than any single source. Coding schemes make that comparison transparent.

modules.i: Regression is a tool for holding other things equal.
modules.a: Interpret a regression table and identify one specification problem.
modules.l: A coefficient describes the association between a variable and the outcome holding the included controls constant. If relevant confounders are absent, that descriptive claim is all the model supports.

modules.i: Institutional data has politics built into its categories.
modules.a: Compile a source audit for three indicators in your proposal.
modules.l: Cross-national data is assembled by national bureaucracies with different definitions. Comparing requires documenting those definitions, because a change in measurement can look exactly like a change in the world.

modules.i: Research design includes obligations to subjects and readers.
modules.a: Complete an ethics checklist for your proposed study.
modules.l: Validity threats are design problems, not execution problems: they must be anticipated. Ethics approval is the formal step, but the substantive obligation is to minimise harm and to report methods honestly enough to be checked.

modules.i: The proposal is the deliverable that ties the module together.
modules.a: Submit a 2,000-word research proposal with a reflection on limitations.
modules.l: A proposal is judged on alignment: question, concept, case and method must point the same way. Stating limitations honestly strengthens a proposal, because it shows the design was chosen rather than inherited.

courses.title: Quantitative Methods for Global Affairs
courses.description: Applied statistics for international affairs: description, inference, regression and panel data, taught through replication exercises on real cross-national datasets.
objectives: Summarise and visualise data appropriately
Interpret significance tests without overclaiming
Estimate and diagnose a multiple regression
Report quantitative results transparently
prerequisites: Research Design in the Social Sciences

modules.i: Most analysis time is spent making data usable.
modules.a: Clean the supplied dataset and submit the log of transformations.
modules.l: Cleaning decisions are analytical decisions: how missingness is handled changes the estimates. A written log makes those choices inspectable and reproducible.

modules.i: Averages conceal the distributions that matter.
modules.a: Produce a descriptive table with justified choices of statistics.
modules.l: The mean is informative only when the distribution is roughly symmetric; with heavy skew it misleads. Reporting median and interquartile range alongside is a safeguard, not a formality.

modules.i: Inference depends on assumptions about how the data were generated.
modules.a: Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a supplied estimate.
modules.l: A confidence interval describes the procedure's long-run behaviour, not the probability that a particular interval contains the truth. That distinction matters when results are reported to non-specialists.

modules.i: Significance is neither effect size nor importance.
r: Wasserstein and Lazar, 'ASA Statement on p-Values'
modules.a: Critique three reported findings for inferential errors.
modules.l: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null is true; it is not the probability the null is true. Conflating the two produces confident claims from weak evidence.

modules.i: The line of best fit summarises association and error.
modules.a: Estimate and interpret a bivariate model on the supplied data.
modules.l: The slope gives the expected change in the outcome per unit of the predictor, with all its limits: functional form, outliers and omitted variables all appear in the residuals.

modules.i: Controls change interpretations, not just numbers.
modules.a: Run the assigned models and report diagnostics for each.
modules.l: Coefficients in a multiple regression are conditional on the other variables included. Adding a control can reverse a sign, which is informative rather than embarrassing: it locates the confounding.

modules.i: Panel structure allows each unit to serve as its own comparison.
r: Angrist and Pischke, Mostly Harmless Econometrics, ch. 5
Course note on fixed effects in practice
modules.a: Estimate a fixed-effects model and explain what it does and does not control.
modules.l: Fixed effects remove time-invariant differences between units, which eliminates a large class of confounders. They do not control for anything that changes over time, so the identifying assumption remains.

modules.i: Graphics should reveal the comparison, not decorate it.
modules.a: Produce three figures and a 300-word results section for the assigned model.
modules.l: Truncated axes and aggregated series can produce a finding visually that does not exist numerically. Uncertainty should be shown, and every figure must be interpretable without the surrounding text.

courses.title: Global Governance and International Organisations
courses.description: How collective problems are governed without world government: the UN system, Bretton Woods institutions, trade governance, NGOs and the persistent questions of legitimacy, accountability and reform.
objectives: Explain governance beyond the state
Compare the mandates of major international organisations
Assess legitimacy and accountability deficits
Evaluate reform proposals

modules.i: Governance is about coordination, and states are not its only authors.
r: Keohane and Nye, 'Introduction' to Governance in a Globalizing World
modules.a: Map the actors governing one issue area and note where authority is unclear.
modules.l: Global governance describes the rules, institutions and practices that coordinate behaviour in the absence of hierarchy. Its analytical payoff is that it directs attention to informal authority as well as formal mandate.

modules.i: One organisation, many bodies, uneven authority.
r: UN Charter, Chapters IV, VII, XV
Course note on UN reform proposals
modules.a: Analyse a Security Council resolution for the authority it relies on.
modules.l: The UN combines a universal assembly with a restricted executive. That design produces legitimacy without enforcement capacity, and enforcement without universal consent.

modules.i: Financial governance was designed for a world that no longer exists.
o: Explain IMF and World Bank mandates
modules.a: Analyse a lending programme for the balance of authority between lender and borrower.
modules.l: Voting weights tied to quotas give creditor states structural influence, which is why reform debates are about shares rather than mandates. Conditionality converts financial leverage into policy influence.

modules.i: The only global regime with binding dispute settlement.
r: Course note on WTO dispute settlement
modules.a: Analyse a trade dispute through the WTO's legal framework.
modules.l: The WTO's authority rested on enforceable adjudication. When the appellate body ceased to function, the regime lost its distinctive feature, and power-based bargaining returned in its place.

modules.i: Regional bodies often deliver what global ones cannot.
r: Case study: an African regional organisation
modules.a: Compare two regional organisations on enforcement and scope.
modules.l: Regional organisations succeed where preferences are closer and monitoring is cheaper. Overlapping membership then becomes functional: states use different venues for different purposes, at the cost of coherence.

modules.i: Non-state actors set agendas and monitor commitments.
r: Keck and Sikkink, Activists Beyond Borders, ch. 1
modules.a: Assess an advocacy campaign's strategy and its evidence of impact.
modules.l: Advocacy networks are powerful when they control information that governments need and can distribute it to audiences that matter. Their weakness is representativeness: nobody elects them.

modules.i: Institutions that make binding decisions need justification.
modules.a: Assess one institution's legitimacy on both dimensions with evidence.
modules.l: Input legitimacy rests on participation and consent; output legitimacy on results. International institutions usually rely on the second, which is fragile precisely when results disappoint.

modules.i: Students design and defend an institutional reform.
modules.a: Submit a reform proposal for one institution, with a coalition analysis.
modules.l: Reform proposals fail when they ignore the interests that sustain the status quo. A serious proposal names the blocking coalition and explains what would change its calculation.

courses.title: Climate Governance and the Energy Transition
courses.description: The governance of climate change and the energy transition: the Paris architecture, carbon markets, green finance, adaptation finance and the domestic politics of decarbonisation.
objectives: Explain climate change as a collective action problem
Assess the Paris Agreement's architecture
Evaluate carbon pricing and market mechanisms
Analyse transition politics in a national case

modules.i: The atmosphere is a commons and the harm is deferred.
modules.a: Model a two-country mitigation game and identify conditions for cooperation.
modules.l: Climate cooperation is hard because costs are immediate and concentrated while benefits are diffuse and delayed. Discount rates therefore do normative work: they decide how much present sacrifice counts as rational.

modules.i: A bottom-up architecture replaced a top-down one.
r: Course note on the global stocktake
modules.a: Assess whether the Paris architecture can deliver the temperature goal, with evidence.
modules.l: Paris achieved breadth by abandoning binding targets for nationally determined pledges and a five-year ratchet. The design trades legal force for participation, which shifts the burden onto domestic politics and transparency.

modules.i: Prices internalise harm, if the price is credible.
o: Compare carbon taxes and emissions trading
r: Course note on carbon pricing instruments
Case study: an emissions trading scheme
modules.a: Design a carbon pricing instrument for a supplied economy and justify the design.
modules.l: Taxes provide price certainty, trading provides quantity certainty; neither guarantees political durability. Offsets weaken integrity unless additionality is verified, which is why market design is contentious.

modules.i: Decarbonisation is a structural change in energy systems.
r: Course note on just transition policy
modules.a: Build a policy package for one sector and identify its distributional effects.
modules.l: Transitions are won on deployment and grids, not on targets. The politics is distributional: workers and regions attached to incumbents must be addressed, or the coalition for change collapses.

modules.i: Capital allocation is a governance instrument.
r: Course note on green bond standards
modules.a: Assess a green bond framework for credibility and use of proceeds.
modules.l: Disclosure makes climate risk legible to markets, but voluntary frameworks invite selective reporting. Credibility depends on standardisation and on third-party verification with consequences.

modules.i: Some impacts are now unavoidable, which raises distributive questions.
o: Distinguish adaptation from loss and damage
r: Course note on the loss and damage fund
modules.a: Assess the adequacy of adaptation finance for one vulnerable region.
modules.l: Adaptation finance is small relative to need and largely loan-based, which adds debt to vulnerability. Loss and damage addresses the residual harm, and its politics is about who pays and who decides.

modules.i: Cities, regions and firms govern alongside states.
r: Course note on transnational climate initiatives
Case study: a city network pledge
modules.a: Map the governing actors for one policy area and assess coordination.
modules.l: Subnational and private initiatives can move faster than treaties and build proof of concept. Their weakness is aggregation: without accounting rules, pledges cannot be summed into a global trajectory.

modules.i: Students negotiate a decision text under a mandate.
r: Simulation pack: mandates and draft decision
modules.a: Negotiate and submit the decision text with a strategy report.
modules.l: Climate negotiations turn on differentiation: who acts first, who pays, and who verifies. The strategy report must show how the delegation protected its mandate without blocking the text.
